newsitem.title: USA: Dow gyrates to record as IBM shares scream higher.
newsitem.headline: Dow gyrates to record as IBM shares scream higher.

text.p: The Dow industrials gyrated to their eighth consecutive record closing high on Friday as Dow component IBM screamed higher to its best finish since before the 1987 stock market crash.

"IBM is a bellwether for the market, which has been roaring along. But just because it's trading at levels near before the '87 crash doesn't mean we're going into a tailspin anytime soon," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
The Dow surged 35 to about 6348.
The blue chip index had bounced between a gain of 65 points and virtually unchanged, spurred by the double witching expiration of November stock index options and equity options.
The Dow climbed about 128 points for the week after last week's 198-point jump.

The string of Dow records sent Wall Street historians scouring the books for a longer stint, but no answers could be found by late Friday. A few guessed a longer recent run would have been in the months leading to the October 1987 crash.
Meanwhile, IBM rallied 8-1/8 to 145, giving the Dow a 25- point boost. IBM shares last ended above 140 October 15, 1987.

IBM's ascent was aided by Merrill Lynch analyst Daniel Mandresh who raised his 12-month IBM price target to $195 from $155. The analyst cited his preliminary checks for the computer giant's fourth-quarter outlook as helping in his latest assessment. "Mandresh is considered to be 'Mr. IBM,' so when he talks, investors listen," Orlando said.

As for the overall market, Abby Joseph Cohen, co-chair of Goldman Sachs' investment policy committee, said the outlook for U.S. stocks remains "constructive. The fundamental support for the market is good. We think prices can go higher since we're in the midst of a long-lasting period of growth."
"It may not be as vigorous as we've seen but it's rapid enough," Cohen added. She noted that inflation remains under control and the recent bond rally is helping stocks.
The Nasdaq Composite fell from record peaks, off nine to 1262 as recent weakness in bellwether Intel cast a pall over that market. Intel lost four to 115-7/8, off six percent since Wednesday.

The S&P 500 rose two to about 738, its second straight all-time high finish. The NYSE Composite rose one to 390. Winners beat losers 12-11 on very heavy NYSE volume of about 525 million shares, swollen by double witching.
Like many other analysts, William LeFevre, a senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum, was surprised by the length and strength of the Dow's latest streak.
"I'm surprised it continues unchecked for this long. We've only had one down Dow day this month" on November 1, he said.

"Does this run mean that Wall Street likes the re-election of (President Bill) Clinton? No. It means we're relieved you have one party in the White House and another in Congress and one will act as a restraint to the other. There'll be no excessive liberal or conservative moves. ... Corporate America is not obstructed and that's the way they look at it."
Among individual issues, Vimpel-Communications, the Russian wireless telecommunications company, jumped 8-1/2 to 29 in its Wall Street debut.

Dow component Texaco added 2-3/4 to 101-1/8. The company confirmed after the close that it settled a racial discrimination lawsuit. The suit had led to calls by black civil rights leaders to boycott Texaco stations and to begin picketing the company on Saturday.
Health Management tumbled 7-5/8 to 14-1/2 after the company issues a profit warning, the latest in a string from health information services companies.

ITI Technologies plunged 60 percent or 18-3/16 points to 11-15/16 after news its single largest customer, ADT Security Systems, said it will reduce purchase orders during the first quarter of 1997. Dain Bosworth cut ITI to hold from buy.
Heartland Wireless slumped 6-1/2 to 12-5/8 after reporting a narrower quarterly loss. Alex Brown cut the stock to buy.

Amgen fell one to 58-5/8 after the Wall Street Journal reported on a study that weight-loss drug leptin may cause diabetes. Amgen rejected the study, saying the test was conducted on cells in a petri dish and had no bearing on living animals.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 8.56 to 1261.80.
The S&P 500 index rose 1.74 to 737.62, a record.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721.
